title: DNA replication; ATP; Water; Plant transport: xylem and transpiration; Inorganic ions
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM11#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; GE01b#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE01b#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM01a#N.4a, BM01b#N.4a, BM11#N.2, BM12#N.7, EX10a#N.2, EX10b#N.6, GE01b#N.7, BM01a#N.5b, BM01b#N.15a, BM11#N.5a, BM12#N.12, EX10a#N.7.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Inorganic phosphate
items.clue: The product released alongside ADP when ATP reacts with water

items.label: Hybrid DNA
items.clue: Intermediate band: one ¹⁵N strand paired with one ¹⁴N strand.

items.label: Density gradient
items.clue: Spun salt solution in which DNA settles at its own level, heavier DNA lower down.

items.label: Dispersive model
items.clue: Idea that old and new DNA are mixed in pieces along every strand; refuted at generation 2.

questions.stem: Why is each covalent bond between oxygen and hydrogen in a water molecule polar?

options.text: The shared electrons are drawn more strongly towards the oxygen atom.
Each hydrogen atom gives up its electron completely to the oxygen atom.
It is a hydrogen bond, and hydrogen bonds are polar by their nature.
Oxygen and hydrogen atoms behave as opposite magnetic poles.

questions.explanation: Oxygen attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen does, so the electrons are shared unequally: oxygen becomes δ− and each hydrogen δ+.

questions.stem: Transpiration puts the column of water in a xylem vessel under tension. Why does the column not break as it is pulled upwards?

options.text: Root pressure pushes the column upwards from below.
Capillary action lifts the water inside the narrow vessel.
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules to each other.
Hydrogen bonds within each molecule resist the pull.

questions.explanation: Cohesion due to hydrogen bonding keeps the molecules attached to one another, so the tension created by evaporation in the leaves is passed down the whole column without it separating.

questions.stem: Which statement about ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is correct?

options.text: It is a nucleotide: adenine and ribose joined to a chain of three phosphate groups.
It is a small protein that binds energy released from glucose in respiration.
It is the cell's main long-term reserve of energy, built up like glycogen.
It is destroyed once used and is rebuilt from glucose rather than from ADP.

questions.explanation: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells.

questions.stem: Which molecules need phosphate ions to be built?

options.text: DNA, RNA and ATP: each contains phosphate groups.
DNA and RNA only: phosphate is used in nucleic acids alone.
Proteins: phosphate is part of every amino acid.
None: phosphate ions are broken down for energy, like a food.

questions.explanation: The nucleotide backbone of DNA and RNA alternates sugar and phosphate; ATP carries three phosphates.

questions.stem: Why is transpiration described as a consequence of gas exchange rather than as a process the leaf carries out for its own sake?

options.text: The plant opens its stomata in order to lose water, because transpiration is needed to pull water up through the xylem.
Stomata must be open for carbon dioxide to enter, and water vapour inevitably diffuses out through the same pores.
Water vapour escapes across the cuticle and epidermis wherever gases are exchanged over the leaf surface.
Transpiration is evaporation that depends only on temperature, so it happens whether or not the stomata are open.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, which can only enter through open stomata. While they are open, water vapour from the saturated air spaces diffuses out down its concentration gradient to the drier atmosphere; the water loss is an unavoidable side effect of gas exchange.

questions.stem: In a potometer, the capillary tube has a radius of 0.40 mm. The air bubble moves 30 mm in 10 minutes. What is the rate of water uptake?

options.text: 3.8 mm³ min⁻¹
15 mm³ min⁻¹
1.5 mm³ min⁻¹
6.0 mm³ min⁻¹

questions.explanation: Volume = πr²l = π × 0.40² × 30 = 15 mm³. Rate = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 mm³ min⁻¹.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule in which both strands contain only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) is replicated three times in a medium that supplies only light nitrogen (¹⁴N), producing 8 DNA molecules. How many of the 8 DNA molecules contain any ¹⁵N?

options.text: 1 of 8
8 of 8
2 of 8
4 of 8

questions.explanation: In round 1 the two ¹⁵N strands separate and each pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand. They stay intact in every later round, so after round 3, 2 molecules contain ¹⁵N and 6 contain only ¹⁴N.

questions.stem: The model shows three water molecules. The symbols δ+ and δ− show partial charges. Which statement correctly describes the interaction labelled 2 in the model?

options.text: An attraction between the partially positive H of one molecule and the partially negative O of another
A covalent bond in which the H atom of one molecule shares a pair of electrons with the O atom of another
An ionic bond between an H⁺ ion in one molecule and an O²⁻ ion in a second, neighbouring molecule
A strong bond, stronger than line 1, that holds the two water molecules in a fixed position

questions.stem: In a transpiring tree, an air bubble forms in one xylem vessel and fills a short length of it. Water in that vessel stops rising, although neighbouring vessels keep working. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Root pressure from the roots can no longer push the water up past the bubble.
The gas breaks the hydrogen-bonded column, so the pull is not passed on.
Water above the bubble can no longer adhere to the lignified vessel wall.
The bubble blocks the supply of ATP that the vessel uses to move water upwards.

questions.explanation: Tension from the leaves travels down the vessel only through a continuous, cohesive column. A gas gap breaks it, so the water below is no longer pulled.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a life process that ATP supplies with energy?

options.text: Water entering a root hair cell by osmosis uses ATP to cross the membrane against its gradient.
Joining amino acids into a polypeptide releases energy, which the cell holds as ATP.
Chromosomes move to the poles in mitosis without ATP, pulled by spindle fibres as they get shorter.
Pumping sodium ions out of a neuron against their concentration gradient uses ATP directly.

questions.explanation: Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium–potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.

questions.stem: Chlorophyll has a magnesium ion at its centre. Haem, in haemoglobin, has an iron ion at its centre. Both ions carry a 2+ charge. A plant short of magnesium is given extra iron ions instead. What happens to its yellowing leaves?

options.text: They turn green, as the extra ions are food that gives the plant energy to make chlorophyll.
They turn green, as the plant converts some of the extra iron into the magnesium it lacks.
They turn green once the plant photosynthesises, as plants make their own minerals as well as their own food.
They stay yellow, as chlorophyll needs magnesium specifically; iron ions cannot take its place.

questions.stem: Why are the walls of xylem vessels thickened with lignin?

options.text: To seal the vessel completely so that no water can escape through the side walls into surrounding cells.
To provide the mitochondria and cytoplasm of the vessel with a surface on which to generate ATP for transport.
To hold the plant upright, which is the only function that lignin has anywhere in the xylem.
To withstand the tension in the water column so that the vessel is not pulled inwards and collapsed.

questions.explanation: The negative pressure potential generated by transpiration would suck a soft-walled tube flat. Lignified walls are rigid enough to withstand these tensions, keeping the vessel open for unimpeded flow; they also contribute to supporting the plant.
